national.title: Did GOP efforts to redistrict the House turn into a dummymander?
national.summary: Republicans undertook a historic effort to redraw several states' congressional districts mid-decade in an attempt to maintain control of the House.
national.body: Republicans undertook a historic effort to redraw several states' congressional districts mid-decade in an attempt to maintain control of the House. That effort was rebuffed on election night as the GOP was on track to lose many of the districts it tried to gerrymander last year. There were several reasons that states undertook what had previously been a rare practice of mid-decade redistricting. Republican efforts started when President Trump ordered Texas lawmakers to redraw their map to net up to five seats for the GOP. But despite the all-out effort, Democrats won control of the House and are on track to win at least 258 House seats, flipping dozens of GOP-held districts.With the House decisively swinging toward Democrats and Democrats undertaking measures in a few states to counter the GOP's efforts, Republicans are faced with the possibility of having created a so-called "dummymander," a situation in which a party tries to gerrymander, but ends up benefiting the other party. national.title: Wendy's "pricing scheme" inflated menu prices, lawsuit alleges
national.summary: In a proposed class action, a California resident alleges that Wendy's conspired with its franchisees to set and raise menu prices.
national.body: A proposed class-action lawsuit alleges that Wendy's engaged in a pricing scheme that reduced competition across its restaurants, driving up costs for customers. The lawsuit, filed Monday in a Maryland district court, accuses the burger chain of conspiring with independently owned franchisees to set and raise prices at its U.S. locations over a six-year period between 2016 and 2022. Wendy's collected "competitively sensitive information" from franchisee locations, including transaction data, to coordinate prices, according to the lawsuit.The lawsuit was filed by Andy Garcia, a California resident and longtime Wendy's customer, according to the suit. He alleges that Wendy's engaged in "anticompetitive conduct" that resulted in artificially high prices, causing him to pay more than he otherwise would have. Garcia also sued NCR Voyix, a software company that provides Aloha POS, a point-of-sale system used by Wendy's."By delegating pricing decisions to a common decision-maker, it eliminates critical price competition that drives costs down for consumers," Blake Hunter Yagman, the lawyer representing Garcia and founding partner of Yagman PLLC, a class-action law firm headquartered in New York, said in an email. "This is even more important with respect to food prices, which have never been higher â and Wendy's owes [it to] its consumers to compete on the merits for better service, more innovative products and better pricing," Yagman added.Wendy's and NCR Voyix did not immediately respond to requests for comment. As of September, Wendy's had 432 company-owned restaurants and 6,762 franchisees across the U.S., according to the company's most recent regulatory filing.In 2024, Wendy's raised concerns after saying it would test Uber-style pricing. Also known as dynamic pricing, that approach allows companies to set prices based on real-time market conditions and other factors such as weather. Other restaurants have also faced scrutiny over their pricing practices. Last month, a consumer sued McDonald's over the use of an AI tool that recommends dynamic pricing.

national.title: Australia set to pass online safety laws with multibillion-dollar fines for tech giants
national.summary: The Australian government clinched a political deal on Tuesday to introduce online safety laws that could expose tech giants to multibillion-dollar fines for failing to prevent foreseeable online harms.
national.body:
MELBOURNE, Australia (AP) — The Australian government clinched a political deal on Tuesday to introduce online safety laws that could expose tech giants to multibillion-dollar fines for failing to prevent foreseeable online harms. The United States warned that the legislation would lead to censorship of lawful speech.

The Digital Duty of Care Bill would require Big Tech to proactively reduce the risk of harm before it occurs, according to an Australian government statement.

The legislation is similar to the European Union's Digital Services Act, passed in 2022, and the United Kingdom's Online Safety Act passed a year later.

The proposed legislation would set minimum safety standards for online services, including games, apps and artificial intelligence chatbots, requiring them to protect Australians from seriously harmful material and conduct, the government said.

"We can't cure the internet, but this is providing some basic safety standards and saying if you build it, you are responsible for its risks," Communications Minister Anika Wells told reporters at Parliament House in Canberra.

Wells announced on Tuesday her center-left Labor Party government had accepted amendments proposed by the minor Greens party to get the legislation through the Senate, where no party holds a majority.

Greens leader David Shoebridge confirmed his party had agreed to support the amended bill.

"Today we are taking power back from a handful of billionaire-owned, largely U.S. corporations and giving it back to Australians who have been paying too high a price for their profits," Shoebridge said in a statement.

Someone had made the threat using the online chat platform Discord. The teen came outside and stood by the doorway. He repeatedly denied making the threat. "Maybe they misheard somebody else," he said. After the interview, the officers left. "Alright, well, look, Colt, I appreciate it. Your dad's got my card… if you hear anything, tell your dad," one of the officers said. That year, Colin Gray gave his son an AR-15 rifle as a Christmas present.Nine months later, the teen brought the rifle to Apalachee High School and opened fire, killing classmates Mason Schermerhorn and Christian Angulo, and teachers Richard Aspinwall and Cristina Irimie, and injuring nine others.In July, the teen was sentenced to life in prison. His father, Colin Gray, received a 15-year sentence for ignoring the warning signs and buying the weapon. national.title: Democrats supporting abortion rights won big in midterms, but vast changes unlikely soon
national.summary: States with bans will still have enough Republicans in power to likely block any repeal attempts for now.
national.body:
Geoff Mulvihill, Associated Press Geoff Mulvihill, Associated Press

Democrats who ran on abortion rights platforms won big in elections for Congress and state government offices. But it's not likely that they'll be able to impose quick and vast abortion policy changes.

That's because Democrats did not take full control of the legislatures and governor's offices in states with the strictest laws — those that ban abortion at six weeks or all stages of pregnancy.

And in Congress, Democrats who will control both the House and Senate could attempt to bar states from adopting some kinds of abortion bans, but any move would likely meet a veto from President Donald Trump, which couldn't be overridden without GOP help.

Abortion has been primarily a state government issue since the U.S. Supreme Court's 2022 ruling that struck down Roe v. Wade allowed states to enforce bans. Now, 13 states ban abortion at all stages of pregnancy — with some exceptions — and four more do so after about the first six weeks.

In 2027, Democrats will have control of both legislative chambers and the governor's office in six states where they currently share power with Republicans. Those states — Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin — already allow abortion through until at least fetal viability, which is generally considered to be sometime after 21 weeks of pregnancy.

Abortion is currently allowed through the first 20 weeks from fertilization, or about 22 weeks' gestation in Wisconsin and 23 in Pennsylvania. Democrats kept the governorships and gained full power in the legislatures in the elections in both states.

Wisconsin Gov.-elect David Crowley and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro are both calling for leveraging that power to amend their states' constitutions to create a right to abortion.

national.summary: Freedom and Feathers were introduced on Monday at the Willard InterContinental in Washington, where the two stayed in a suite leading up to their trip to the White House.
national.body: Washington — President Trump pardoned two turkeys, Freedom and Feathers, on Tuesday, continuing one of the White House's most anticipated holiday traditions.Mr. Trump said Tuesday that he is granting the turkeys "full, absolute and unconditional pardon — meaning they will live forever.""Freedom, as of this moment, you have a complete and total pardon," Mr. Trump told one of the turkeys. The president said the other turkey, Feathers, had run off into the bushes but would still be pardoned.Freedom and Feathers were introduced on Monday at the Willard InterContinental in Washington, where the two have been staying in a suite leading up to their trip to the White House.This year's festivities will mark the 79th annual National Thanksgiving Turkey Presentation. The event dates back to 1947, when the National Turkey Federation first began presenting turkeys to then-President Harry Truman, although the presidential pardon didn't become a tradition until 1989, under President George H.W. Bush.How Freedom and Feathers were chosenMr. Trump introduced Freedom and Feathers on Tuesday, noting he felt their names are "good, but I've heard better. It's pretty out there." This year's turkeys were raised by Scott and Becky Rightsell in Fort Sybert, West Virginia. national.title: Can Jensen Huang put out the fire he started at Nvidia?
national.summary: Despite Jensen Huang's shock return as Nvidia's CEO, experts say it's anything but business as usual for the chipmaker.
national.body: Jensen Huang's first task in returning to lead Nvidia after resigning last week under a cloud will be to deal with the fallout from his stunning exit and even more surprising reprieve. Following his reinstatement by the company's board, some lawmakers are calling for investigations into President Trump's role in the billionaire entrepreneur's return and whether Nvidia skirted export rules meant to prevent its advanced chips from reaching China. And while Huang may be viewed as key to Nvidia's success, his return raises a thicket of legal and operational problems, according to financial and governance experts."Three tests will now decide how strongly it builds from here: how its leadership sits with Washington, how it handles China and how long AI spending keeps growing at this speed," said Nigel Green, CEO of deVere Group, an investment advisory firm, in an email. national.title: DR Congo says military aircraft missing as rebels claim to shoot down plane
national.summary: A South African fighter pilot and a Ugandan officer are reportedly among those aboard the downed plane.
national.body:
The Democratic Republic of Congo military says it is searching for one of its aircraft, after rebels said they had shot down a warplane in the east.

The military said it had lost contact with a small Cessna 208 cargo plane on Sunday following "poor weather conditions". The fate of the plane and its crew remained uncertain, it added.

On the same day, the rebel Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN) said it had shot down a plane of the same type that was on a mission to bomb Minembwe in South Kivu province.

Four people were reportedly on board, including a Ugandan and a South African pilot, who is said to have been captured alive.

On Tuesday, the FRN said the plane they had shot down was a Cessna 208, which had been "converted into a light attack aircraft" enabling it "to carry and launch precision-guided bombs and missiles".

Its wreckage now lies 10km (6 miles) from Minembwe, a rebel statement said, adding that a Ugandan and South African "mercenaries" had been captured.

The BBC has not independently verified the rebel claim, or whether the aircraft reported missing by the DR Congo military is the same one the rebels say they shot down.

South Africa's government has not commented, while Uganda's military has denied any involvement.

national.summary: The warrant application covers a 46-year period beginning in 1980, long before Omar was in Congress, according to newly released court records. The documents are heavily redacted, and no criminal charges are listed.

national.title: Nigerian monarch, 92, suspended after sexual assault claims
national.summary: The Emir of Daura is one of Nigeria's best-known monarchs, with politicians often trying to gain his support.
national.body:
One of Nigeria's best-known monarchs, the Emir of Daura, has been suspended from all official engagements and travel following allegations of sexual assault by a Polish tourist.

The visitor said Umar Farouk Umar, 92, had grabbed her chest during a tourism encounter and that she felt disgusted by the experience.

The allegation sparked widespread discussion across social media platforms, with many calling for the suspension of the emir and an investigation - calls the Katsina state government has now heeded.

Umar has not commented on the allegations or his suspension.

He is one of several emirs - a traditional role dating back to pre-colonial times - who still wield great cultural and religious influence in northern Nigeria, although they have lost their political power.

Daura, where Umar serves as emir, holds an extremely important position for the Hausa people who dominate northern Nigeria. It is widely regarded as their spiritual homeland and the origin of the Hausa royal lineage, serving as the core of Hausa origin mythology and the legitimate foundation of traditional authority.

Politicians routinely visit his palace for royal prayers and to gain his support.

On her Instagram page, the tourist said she had spent 30 days travelling around Nigeria before visiting the Emir's palace on 14 November.

national.title: Do you need a power of attorney if you already have a will?
national.summary: A will is an important part of estate planning, but it may leave some critical financial decisions unaddressed.
national.body: Having a will in place can make a difficult time easier for your loved ones. A will gives you a say in how your assets are distributed after your death, helps prevent disputes over your estate and provides other important guidance for the people you leave behind — yet recent research from USAA shows that just 19% of Americans have a will or estate plan in place. And even a carefully written will can have limitations.For example, what happens if you're seriously injured or become too ill to manage your finances? Your bills and other financial obligations won't disappear, and someone may need to step in to handle them — but a will can be limited help in those cases. Being a spouse, adult child or named executor doesn't automatically give someone the legal authority to make those decisions, after all. That's why it's worth looking beyond your will when evaluating your estate plan. Another legal document, known as a power of attorney, can play an important role in protecting your finances under certain circumstances. But do you actually need one if you've already written a will? That's what we'll examine below.Find out about the life insurance options you have with USAA.Do you need a power of attorney if you already have a will?In most cases, having both a will and a power of attorney is a smart move because these documents address different situations. A will generally determines what happens to your assets after you die, while a power of attorney allows someone you choose to act on your behalf while you're still alive. Here's why that distinction matters:A will doesn't give anyone authority over your finances while you're aliveA common misconception is that naming an executor in your will gives that person the ability to manage your financial affairs whenever necessary. In reality, an executor's authority generally begins after your death and after any required court appointment. That means your executor typically can't use your will to access your bank accounts, pay your mortgage or handle other financial matters if you're hospitalized or become incapacitated.Without another legal arrangement in place, your family may have to seek court authorization to manage certain financial responsibilities on your behalf. national.title: US attorney general dodges questions about Nvidia investigation
national.summary: Nvidia's share price have fallen 7% as lawmakers demand answers about President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's reinstatement.
national.body:
US Attorney General Todd Blanche has backed Nvidia as a "good corporate citizen" while refusing to comment on whether it was being investigated by the administration.

Blanche said he had no information about Jensen Huang's security clearance status, as lawmakers demand answers about President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's reinstatement as the AI microchip maker's chief executive.

Huang was given his job back less than two weeks after being forced to resign over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

Asked several times on Tuesday if the justice department or FBI had investigated Huang, Blanche responded: "I don't know what you're talking about."

Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where he will be questioned over his relationship with a former executive for Megaspeed - the alleged China spy - due to national security concerns.

The US commerce department has also announced it was preparing to blacklist tech company Megaspeed, the Singapore-based Nvidia customer that has been suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China.

In a joint statement last week, the commerce and justice departments said they began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations" .

But speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Blanche said the latter department has "hundreds, if not more" export investigations occurring at any one time.

national.title: Chinese neuroscientist at Princeton held by ICE after detention at D.C. airport
national.summary: The Department of Homeland Security says Xie overstayed her visa and did not have authorization to study in the U.S. Xie's lawyer says she has a pending asylum application.
national.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A Chinese neuroscience researcher at Princeton University is in the custody of immigration authorities after she was detained while trying to get on a flight back from Washington, marking another instance of federal enforcement at airports.

Eva Yi Xie, a third-year doctoral student at Princeton, was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport on Thursday as she tried to fly back to New Jersey from a conference in the nation's capital, her university adviser Carlos Brody said in a social media post.

The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, says Xie overstayed her visa and did not have authorization to study in the United States.

"News of Eva's detention is distressing for me and many members of the Princeton University community," Rodney Priestley, dean of the university's graduate school, said in a statement. "We hope Eva will soon be able to resume her studies at Princeton."

Two days after Xie was taken into custody in Washington, masked immigration officers detained a father and daughter on an airport jet bridge in Seattle. ICE has ramped up detentions at airports since the summer, especially targeting people it says have overstayed their visas.

Kerry Doyle, Xie's lawyer, said she came to the U.S. at age 14 with her family from China and has had an asylum application pending for years. Doyle insisted that Xie has permission to live, work and study in the U.S. while her case is pending.

Doyle said Xie is being held in ICE's Caroline Detention Center in Virginia.

DHS said in a statement that Xie came to the United States on a temporary visa on March 16, 2016, but "chose to violate our nation's laws by refusing to depart by the required date of September 15, 2016."

national.title: Beloved drive-thru worker on making a year's salary on last day of work
national.summary: When Sighle Williams decided to retire from Mac's Drive Thru after 37 years, she never could have expected the send-off she received, which is the focus of a new Netflix documentary.
national.body: Sighle Williams keeps it simple. "I just like to treat people the way I like to be treated," she told "CBS Mornings."So when Williams, who'd spent her 37-year career making people smile at Mac's Drive Thru in Gainesville, Florida, was approached about having a documentary made about her last day, she was excited but a bit skeptical.That short film, called "One Last Order," premieres on Netflix Tuesday and has already garnered awards from the Aspen Shortfest, Nantucket Film Festival, Miami Film Festival and more.The movie documents Williams' final day on the job, but it also shows the side of Williams that her beloved customers didn't see, like how she raised five girls â her sister and niece's children â as her own. The film shares how she lived in a house for a while with no running water or electricity."I just did what I needed to do, I knew I needed to make sure they were straight, and I needed to make sure I went to work," she said.When she went to work, she made everyone feel like she was glad to see them. She remembered people's orders.On her last day at Mac's, her boss decided that every dollar made would go back into Williams' pocket as a retirement bonus. Community members lined up around the block and waited for up to four hours to say goodbye and give Williams one final order. The Danish law introduced in 2018 is among Europe's most aggressive attempts to force immigrant communities to assimilate and to avoid the evolution of "parallel societies" in the country. This can involve demolishing buildings, selling properties to private landlords, or converting them to other forms of housing, resulting in the eviction and relocation of some residents.Under the law, non-Western countries include all nations outside the European Union, Andorra, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Monaco, Norway, San Marino, Switzerland, United Kingdom, Vatican State, the U.S., Canada, Australia, New Zealand. national.title: Experts say failed climate talks could worsen inequality, but progress not stalled
national.summary: Dozens of nations objected to the summit's final text because it didn't mention fossil fuels that drive climate change or increase financial help for poorer countries.
national.body:
Tammy Webber, Associated Press Tammy Webber, Associated Press

This year's U.N. climate talks in Turkey failed to deliver consensus on how the world should confront climate change, even as it triggers more natural disasters that hit hardest in vulnerable countries that didn't cause the problem.

Dozens of nations on Sunday objected to the final text — meant to guide climate actions — presented at the summit, called COP31, because it didn't mention fossil fuels, primarily the use of coal, oil and gas that drives climate change. It also didn't include increased financial commitments to help hard-hit nations adapt to a warmer world.

That leaves a lot of questions about what happens next — and what it means for ordinary, everyday people — as scientists warn that the world is on track to exceed goals to limit warming, set in the 2015 Paris Agreement.

Even though there wasn't a final agreement at COP31, climate action is still moving forward, as nations, states, provinces, Indigenous groups and even local officials take action on their own.

That includes a new voluntary initiative on transitioning away from fossil fuels that falls outside of the United Nations' purview. Almost 60 countries participated in the first International Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels in Colombia this year, and the second is scheduled for next year in the island nation of Tuvalu.

Rather than being held back, countries "are building new networks to work together," said climate scientist Katharine Hayhoe from The Nature Conservancy.

She said most climate action takes place below the national level — including in the United States, which did not participate directly in the U.N. climate talks for the second year in a row. Although President Donald Trump pulled the U.S. out of the Paris Agreement, a delegation from the U.S. that included California Gov. Gavin Newsom attended the summit to pledge climate action.

national.title: West Coast king tides could break decades-old records and flood communities
national.summary: In the San Francisco Bay Area, tides could reach 2.6 feet above normal Tuesday before peaking Wednesday at 2.8 feet above normal, said Dial Hoang, a National Weather Service forecaster.
national.body:
Olga R. Rodriguez, Associated Press Olga R. Rodriguez, Associated Press

SAN FRANCISCO (AP) — High tides along the Pacific Coast could break 40-year-old records and flood low-lying coastal communities, complicating travel during Thanksgiving week.

In the San Francisco Bay Area, tides could reach 2.6 feet above normal Tuesday before peaking Wednesday at 2.8 feet above normal, said Dial Hoang, a National Weather Service forecaster.

The Bay Area's highest recorded tide reached 2.9 feet above normal in San Francisco on Jan. 27, 1983, he said. San Francisco's famed Embarcadero waterfront, which flooded during heavy rain last week, is again at risk of flooding.

King tides, the highest tides of the year, occur when the gravitational pull of the moon and sun aligns to raise water levels. Their effects this year are being amplified by the ongoing super El Niño, which has warmed the ocean, leading to an increased volume of seawater.

The weather service issued a high surf warning in the Bay Area on Wednesday, when breaking waves of 20 to 30 feet could overpower swimmers and sweep people into the ocean.

"Remain out of the water and stay off of jetties, piers, and rocks. Never turn your back to the ocean!" the agency said in a social media post.

Heavy rain forecast for Tuesday evening into Wednesday could worsen street flooding.

national.title: Will wind ground your favorite balloon in Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade?
national.summary: Local officials are wary of the balloons getting blown off course and into spectators. Macy's says it'll make the decision Thursday morning.
national.body:
NEW YORK (AP) — The annual Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York City is once again facing what's become its eternal foe: wind.

An incoming storm is expected to bring heavy winds and rain to the region, and the parade's iconic character balloons — which have graced the canyons between Manhattan's skyscrapers for decades — could be grounded if it gets too windy.

The city has long had measures in place that dictate whether to lower balloons or cancel their flights entirely, with local officials wary of strong winds knocking them off course and into spectators along the parade route.

City rules have long stated that large balloons can't fly if sustained winds exceed 23 mph (37 kph) or gusts exceed 34 mph (55 kph).

These measures were implemented after an accident in 1997 where a balloon careened into a lamppost near Central Park and critically injured a woman.

Brian Hurley, a meteorologist at the National Weather Service, said the parade crowd should be ready for a wet and windy day. But for the balloons, he said, the big headache could be the wind gusts.

Sustained winds will range from 15 to 25 mph (24 to 40 kph), with gusts of 30 to 40 mph (48 to 64 kph) in the morning that could grow stronger in the late afternoon, Hurley said. The parade kicks off at 8:30 a.m.

Hurley also noted that gusts could feel more concentrated because Manhattan's tall buildings often create a wind tunnel effect.

national.title: Trump will give Medal of Freedom to Giuliani, a fierce political ally who led New York through 9/11
national.summary: As President Donald Trump's personal lawyer, he was a central figure in efforts to overturn Trump's 2020 presidential election loss to Democrat Joe Biden.
national.body:
Mike Catalini, Associated Press Mike Catalini, Associated Press

President Donald Trump on Tuesday will award the Medal of Freedom, the nation's highest civilian honor, to former New York Mayor Rudy Giuliani.

Giuliani was hailed for leading New York after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks. Trump has called Giuliani, a fellow New Yorker, the "greatest Mayor in the history of New York City, and an equally great American Patriot."

Giuliani's public life has undergone a rise and fall in recent years. After leading the nation's biggest city through Sept. 11, he mounted a brief campaign for the Republican presidential nomination in 2008, becoming one of the most recognizable U.S. political figures.

As Trump's personal lawyer, he was a central figure in efforts to overturn Trump's 2020 presidential election loss to Democrat Joe Biden. Courts rejected the fraud claims he advanced, and two former Georgia election workers won a $148 million defamation judgment against him.

He was later sanctioned by courts and disbarred in New York and Washington for repeatedly making false statements about the election.

Trump said last year he would award the medal to Giuliani , shortly after he was seriously injured in a car crash .

Giuliani, 82, said in a statement he was honored by the award.

national.summary: BepiColombo was launched as a joint mission between the European Space Agency and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency in October 2018.
national.body: A spacecraft has entered Mercury's orbit after an eight-year journey, overcoming a technical glitch to continue its mission to conduct scientific observations around the planet. BepiColombo was launched as a joint mission between the European Space Agency and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency in October 2018. Since then, it has navigated its way toward Mercury. On Nov. 21, the spacecraft attached itself to Mercury's orbit. The maneuver started with a scheduled, brief loss of contact with the mission control team at the European Space Operations Center in Darmstadt, Germany, the ESA said in a news release. As BepiColombo passed over the planet, it fired four axial thrusters that slowed it enough to lock into Mercury's orbit. During this stage of the mission, the spacecraft came within 400 miles of Mercury's surface. The burn was supposed to last for about 37 minutes. But when the ESA team reestablished contact with BepiColombo, they found the maneuver had been interrupted, causing the spacecraft to enter safe mode, where nonessential activities are stopped. Analysis of trajectory data showed the spacecraft had only completed about 77% of the maneuver. "Upon finding Bepi in safe mode, it was like flipping a switch. Everybody was focused in understanding what had happened," ESA BepiColombo flight operations director Ignacio Tanco said in a statement. The glitch has been traced to a software issue involving attitude guidance and thruster control, the ESA said. The investigation into the error is continuing. Despite the error and the incomplete maneuver, ESA scientists were eventually able to confirm that BepiColombo had locked onto Mercury's orbit. It took six hours from the time the maneuver started to confirm that it had been successful, the ESA said. Over the next few weeks, the spacecraft will continue to make small thruster burns to gradually adjust its orbit around Mercury. Each movement will be adapted by BepiColombo's flight dynamics team using the spacecraft's actual trajectory. This will allow BepiColombo to enter the "optimum point" in orbit. The ESA compared it to "braking a car at just the right moment" to find the "sweet spot." Conducting multiple maneuvers also allows the craft to maximize its fuel supplies. national.body: Officials are searching for a man who went overboard during a cruise vacation on board Royal Caribbean's Allure of the Seas, according to Bahamian officials.The Allure of the Seas is on an eight-day Thanksgiving cruise in the Caribbean that departed from Miami on Sunday. The cruise line called out a passenger's name over the ship's loudspeaker system for several hours before determining that the man had gone overboard, according to passengers on board the cruise ship. national.summary: Hundreds of people from different African countries have been recruited to fight for Russia, according to Ukraine.
national.body:
A Zimbabwean national has been convicted by a court in South Africa of planning to go to fight in Ukraine.

The country has strict laws which restrict unauthorised involvement in overseas wars.

Twenty-four-year-old Wesley Sothole, who pleaded guilty, was handed a five-year suspended prison sentence and was ordered to be deported from South Africa.

He is one of five Zimbabweans who were arrested at OR Tambo Airport in Johannesburg on 8 November. South African prosecutors have not confirmed which side the Zimbabweans allegedly intended to fight for.

Sothole's four co-accused have yet to enter pleas and are due to return to the Kempton Park Magistrates' Court on 1 December for further plea and sentencing proceedings.

Another four Zimbabweans were arrested at a hotel in Johannesburg at the same time in a joint operation and are facing a different court process.

The investigation has involved South African police, Interpol and other international law enforcement agencies.

South Africa's Foreign Military Assistance Act was passed in 1998 at a time when the government was concerned about members of the former apartheid security services going to fight elsewhere in Africa.

national.summary: It is the latest case involving Nicolas Sarkozy who became the first French ex-president to go to jail last year.
national.body:
Nicolas Sarkozy and his wife Carla Bruni-Sarkozy are to face trial next year over charges stemming from the former French president's conviction for conspiring to fund his election campaign with money from late Libyan dictator Muammar Gaddafi.

The charges centre on the retraction of the testimony of a key witness who had initially said he had evidence that could incriminate Sarkozy.

Sarkozy was given a five-year sentence in the case last September and became the first French ex-president to go to jail, even though he only spent 20 days behind bars. He has always denied doing anything wrong in the case and the appeals verdict is expected next Monday.

Since losing his re-election bid in 2012, Sarkozy has faced several criminal investigations.

In 2024, he was handed a one-year sentence – of which six months were suspended – over the illegal financing of his 2012 re-election campaign.

In 2021, he was found guilty of trying to bribe a judge and sentenced to three years in jail – two of them suspended – and thus became the first former French president to get a custodial sentence. He was allowed to serve his time at home wearing a tag instead of going to jail.

The new case centres on a Libyan businessman, Ziad Takieddine, who had said he had written proof that Sarkozy's 2007 campaign bid was "abundantly" financed by Tripoli, and that the €50m (£43m) in payments continued after he became president.

Takieddine, who died last year, withdrew his accusations in an interview in 2020.

Norfolk Police said that officers were called Monday evening to reported "suspicious activity" at an address on the rural estate in eastern England. After a search involving police dogs, drones and a helicopter, two men were arrested on suspicion of burglary and trespassing.

national.summary: Prosecutors say they are pursuing evidence of crimes allegedly committed by the Democratic congresswoman over decades, and unrelated to her work in Congress.
national.body:
A federal court has unsealed heavily redacted documents related to the search of US lawmaker Ilhan Omar's home last month, despite an attempt from prosecutors to block the release.

Some 169 pages of court documents show investigators were looking for potential criminal violations involving Omar going all the way back to 1980.

The Minnesota Democrat, who has not been charged with a crime and has denied any wrongdoing, moved to the US from Somalia in 1995 and became a naturalised citizen in 2000.

Omar, who has been an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump, described the search on social media as "an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement".

After the search of her home in October, immigration agents offered limited details saying it was related to an ongoing federal criminal investigation.

The exchanges in the released court documents show a back-and-forth between a judge and federal prosecutors over executing a warrant and releasing the documents to the public.

Although heavily redacted, the documents offer a glimpse into what the investigation may involve.

The records show the government applied for a warrant to search her Washington DC home for evidence of crimes "involving Ilhan Nur Said Elmi a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar, and occurring between 1980 to the present". The specific offences are redacted in the unsealed documents.

national.title: Trump's intervention on behalf of Jensen Huang gives Democrats more 2028 campaign fuel
national.summary: Still euphoric over their sweeping midterm victories, many ambitious Democrats are still feeling around for the right message on artificial intelligence, which carries both promise and peril as it becomes increasingly intertwined with the economy, infrastructure and daily life.
national.body:
Jonathan J. Cooper, Associated Press Jonathan J. Cooper, Associated Press

For Democrats eyeing the White House, President Donald Trump's coziness with tech executives was already a potent target even before he successfully pressured Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang as chief executive.

Now his extraordinary intervention has crystallized their concerns about the growing power of artificial intelligence companies and his blending of government and business interests.

Huang had lost his job because of extramarital affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of working as a spy for Beijing. Eleven days later, Nvidia's board put him back in charge.

Although Democrats lack a unified vision for how to handle the proliferation of artificial intelligence, the episode was an opportunity for them to speak largely in unison as they called Huang's return a threat to national security and described Trump's role as corrupt.

Nvidia's decision sends a message "that the national security of this country is not as important as your relationship with President Trump," said Sen. Ruben Gallego, an Arizona Democrat considering a White House campaign, in an interview with The Associated Press.

"We also have to figure out how corporate America doesn't take a bad lesson from this, and thinks that somehow it's OK for them to evade national security for the purposes of just selling more," Gallego said.

national.title: Records show how DOJ, judge debated constitutional implications of searching Rep. Ilhan Omar's home
national.summary: The unsealed filings show that U.S. Magistrate Judge Matthew Sharbaugh — before authorizing the search of Omar's home — raised concerns about the "Speech or Debate Clause" implications of searching a private residence belonging to a member of Congress.
national.body:
Michael Kunzelman, Associated Press Michael Kunzelman, Associated Press

WASHINGTON (AP) — A magistrate judge who authorized a recent search of Rep. Ilhan Omar's home by federal agents ruled that the Minnesota Democrat was entitled to assert her right to privacy protections afforded to sitting members of Congress at the outset of the search, according to court documents unsealed on Monday.

The unsealed filings reveal how Justice Department attorneys and U.S. Magistrate Judge Matthew Sharbaugh resolved their initial disagreement over the thorny constitutional implications of searching a member of Congress' private residence for a criminal investigation.

The heavily redacted documents — released in response to a lawsuit filed by media organizations — do not appear to shed new light on the reason or outcome of the search itself or disclose new details of an immigration-fraud investigation that Omar claims is politically motivated.

Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News

Federal authorities are investigating potential fraud in her family's immigration paperwork and have issued grand jury subpoenas to some of her relatives, The Associated Press reported last month, citing a person briefed on the investigation who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss an ongoing investigation.

The unsealed filings show that Sharbaugh — before authorizing the search of Omar's home — raised concerns about the "Speech or Debate Clause" implications of searching a private residence belonging to a member of Congress. The clause, which is designed to protect legislators from executive branch interference or intimidation, includes a privilege against compelled disclosures.

Sharbaugh said he disagreed with the government's argument that the privilege is limited only to official congressional offices and certain electronic devices.

national.title: Francis' private diary reveals pope grappling with spiritual crisis and encounters with the devil
national.summary: Pope Francis saw the "gates of hell" when he realized the depths of the clergy sexual abuse scandal and experienced mystical visions of the devil throughout his ministry, according to excerpts of his personal diary published Tuesday by the Vatican.
national.body:
Nicole Winfield, Associated Press Nicole Winfield, Associated Press

VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Francis saw the "gates of hell" when he realized the depths of the clergy sexual abuse scandal and experienced mystical visions of the devil throughout his ministry, according to excerpts of his personal diary published Tuesday by the Vatican.

"The Private Diary of Pope Francis" also reveals the Argentine pope suffered a profound spiritual crisis in 2021-22, connected to his own temptations to exercise power omnipotently. He overcame the crisis by entrusting himself entirely to God's mercy.

The book, released globally in several languages, offers a deeply personal view of Francis' mind and heart, revealing his innermost fears, insecurities, dreams and temptations. It shows him as incredibly hard on himself, lamenting his own sense of worthlessness and shame, and his utter trust in God to lead him, even from the depths of despair.

Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News

The book was curated by a close aide, Cardinal Víctor Manuel Fernández, the Argentine theologian who heads the Vatican's doctrine office and writes that Francis wanted the papers published. Fernández is listed as the author, as his comments contextualize Francis' diary entries.

Written in a leather-bound calendar used as a notebook, it starts in 1992, when Jorge Mario Bergoglio was auxiliary bishop of Buenos Aires. It continues through his time as cardinal in the Argentine capital and finally pope. The last entry is Aug. 18, 2024.

The most moving sections are Francis' revelations of his own spiritual torments and what he described as encounters with the devil — visceral, tangible and seemingly terrifying visions. Two occurred in Buenos Aires, and the third after his disastrous 2018 trip to Chile.

national.title: Israeli air strike kills Hamas internal security chief in Gaza
national.summary: Naeem Abu Nahel, who had been in the post for two months, is among seven Palestinians reportedly killed in Israeli strikes on Tuesday.
national.body:
At least seven Palestinians, including a senior Hamas security official, have been killed in Israeli air strikes in the Gaza Strip, health officials and first responders say.

Naeem Abu Nahel, the head of Hamas's internal security service, was targeted in western Gaza City, Gaza's Hamas-run interior ministry said. The 50-year-old had only been in the position since September, when his predecessor was captured in a raid by Israeli special forces .

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz announced that Abu Nahel was "eliminated" by the Israeli military.

The six other people were killed in two earlier air strikes elsewhere in Gaza.

Three people, including a teenage boy, were killed in the Wadi Gaza area, south of Gaza City, according to the health officials and first responders. The other three were killed at a police station in the al-Mawasi area, west of Khan Younis, they added.

Gaza's police force, which operates under the interior ministry, said two of its officers were among those who died in the second attack. It also accused Israel of "an ongoing campaign targeting the police apparatus aimed at sowing chaos" in the territory.

The Israeli military said it struck "military operatives" in both areas.

Witnesses said an Israeli drone targeted Naeem Abu Nahel as he was walking on a side street near a tent camp for displaced people in Gaza City.

national.summary: The president has staked the nation's economic growth on artificial intelligence.
national.body:

WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump saw little choice but to fight to reinstate Jensen Huang at AI behemoth Nvidia.

The president has staked the nation's economic growth on artificial intelligence, and worried Huang's ouster was not only tanking the stock market — but also risked putting the U.S. behind Beijing in the race for dominance in the field if Huang, widely seen by backers and critics as a generational talent in artificial intelligence, were to be poached by a Chinese firm.

And the president, a thrice-married man and real estate maven who has seen his own marital infidelity scrutinized in the press, bristled at Huang being ousted from the company he built because of extramarital affairs, including one with an executive at a Singapore-based company who U.S. officials suspect was a Chinese spy.

So Trump engaged in an extraordinary level of behind-the-scenes maneuvering to reinstate Huang, starting almost immediately after the CEO's fall from grace when he resigned on Nov. 12 as reports trickled out about a trio of affairs.

The president stated plainly in a CNBC interview on Monday he used his considerable sway to get Huang his job back. "I spoke to them," Trump said of the company's board of directors. "Let me just put it that way. And I convinced them."

national.title: Land mine casualties soar in Syria, two years after war
national.summary: Nearly 1,000 children are among those killed or injured by explosives left over from the conflict, figures show.
national.body:
Eleven-year-old Alaa was tending her family's goats with her siblings in a field behind their home in Umm Khuzaym, north-west Syria, on Sunday when there was a flash and a deafening bang.

"Then we heard people screaming," Alaa's father, Walid Mohammed Al-Ghafar, told the BBC.

Walid ran outside to find his daughter lying face down, killed, and her 10-year-old brother, Mahmoud, seriously injured.

The incident and others this week bring to nearly 1,000 the number of children killed or injured by explosive ordnance in Syria since the fall of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, according to the UN Mine Action Service (Unmas).

The village is one of many where families have returned to homes and farmland that were once on the front lines of Syria's 13-year civil war.

Alaa's father said demining teams had visited several times to clear the fields. He and other residents believed it was safe for farmers and children to move around.

But mines and other explosives can lie far beyond former battle lines, making it difficult to establish which areas are safe.

"Remnants of war from today's conflicts are often very widely and broadly scattered, often without patterns, which makes it extremely difficult to do clearance," Katrin Atkins, research lead at Landmine Monitor, a global mine monitoring initiative, told the BBC.

national.title: WATCH: Trump holds 2026 White House turkey pardon with Freedom and Feathers
national.summary: Both birds will get a reprieve from ending up on a Thanksgiving dinner table, but only one of them will get a ceremonial pardon at the White House.
national.body:
Mike Catalini, Associated Press Mike Catalini, Associated Press

Two turkeys named Freedom and Feathers are set to get Thanksgiving pardons from President Donald Trump on Tuesday.

Both birds will get a reprieve from ending up on a Thanksgiving dinner table, but only one of them will get a ceremonial pardon at the White House. The public can vote online for which of the West Virginia native birds will get the in-person honor from Trump. Both will live out their days at Texas A&M University.

Tuesday's event will be the 79th turkey pardoning, according to the White House, but the tradition did not become annual until George H.W. Bush's administration in 1989.

Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News

Typically a light-hearted moment before the quintessential American holiday, the turkey pardoning can offer a brief departure from politics and policy.

An early story of presidential turkey pardoning dates to Abraham Lincoln's administration, according to the White House Historical Association, when he granted a reprieve to a bird that was to be served for Christmas dinner after his son Tad intervened on the gobbler's behalf.

Nearly a century later, a photographer captured the moment a smiling Dwight Eisenhower fed a cranberry to a speckled turkey in 1954. In 1963, John F. Kennedy, just days before he was fatally shot in Texas, pardoned a turkey that wore around its neck a sign that said, "Good Eating, Mr. President."

national.title: Who really owns the Albanian land Jared Kushner wants to turn into a 5-star resort?
national.summary: Albania's Prime Minister Edi Rama has vowed that Kushner's resort project will go ahead as planned. But an ongoing investigation by Albania's state prosecutor into forged land titles could halt the project.
national.body:
The sun sets over coastal mountains near the city of Vlore, the region where Jared Kushner plans to build a five-star luxury resort. The land that Kushner bought for this project, though, is claimed by several local Albanians and its ownership is being investigated by state prosecutors. Rob Schmitz/NPR hide caption

ZVERNEC, Albania — In the summer of 2021, Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump boarded a yacht owned by Nat Rothschild, an heir to the European banking family. On the way from Montenegro to Greece, the yacht anchored off the coast of Albania.

And, as Kushner told an investment conference last year, that's when Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama arrived at the boat to tell them about his plan for the country.

"I was very impressed by what he wanted to do with the country," said Kushner. "I really didn't know anything about the country and I didn't understand the history, and the darkness of the history with the communism and terrible leadership led to it being fully undeveloped as a nation."

A year later, Kushner was looking for development opportunities in the Balkans. He returned to the Albanian coast — to the city of Vlore, which was finishing the construction of an airport atop a wetland near an undeveloped coastline. "And obviously, a country's going to build an airport by the coast in a place they think is most beautiful," Kushner told the conference, "so we went there and we were looking for opportunities, and we found some incredible opportunities."

Kushner found those opportunities at Hidrovor Beach, an expanse of caramel-colored sand along the southern Albanian coast, with the gentle waves of the Adriatic lapping its perimeter and a view of an uninhabited island. A company working for Kushner purchased this land and 300 acres surrounding it for more than $130 million in April. But several people here tell NPR this is not Kushner's land.

Gentian Mocka says his family has owned this strip of beach, named Hidrovor Beach, since the time of the Ottoman Empire. The land is now slated to be developed for a luxury hotel owned by Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump. In the background is Sazan Island, a publicly owned island that Trump and Kushner also say they will develop. Rob Schmitz/NPR hide caption

"This land here belonged to my family for centuries," says Gentian Mocka, who claims his family has owned this strip of beach and wetland since the time of the Ottoman Empire. He provided NPR land titles that appear to prove this.

national.title: Army plans to detonate Iowa stockpile on Wednesday, tells public there's no reason to panic
national.summary: The detonation of 68 barrels of lead azide was initially planned for last Friday, but the Army has since changed the date three times following an outpouring of public concern about potential health and environmental effects.
national.body:
Susan Montoya Bryan, Associated Press Susan Montoya Bryan, Associated Press

Laura Bargfeld, Associated Press Laura Bargfeld, Associated Press

MIDDLETOWN, Iowa (AP) — The U.S. Army plans to detonate the nation's entire stockpile of lead azide in Iowa on Wednesday morning, warning that the dangerously degrading bomb-making chemicals could otherwise explode at any time.

"Inaction is no longer an option," said Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, the Army's leader of the operation.

Officials on Tuesday warned nearby residents to be ready to evacuate to avoid toxic dust in the air while also seeking to assure them that barriers around the blast zone should limit much of the plume.

"We don't believe that the public should be in a panic," said Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle. "Our goal is to keep as much of it as we can here on our Iowa Army Ammunition plant to prevent it from traveling."

The controlled detonation of roughly five tons of degraded lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown has set off concerns about potential health and environmental effects and frustration over a lack of information. Experts have advised that the stockpile will become more volatile as temperatures cool in the coming days.

national.summary: Andrei Chibis, head of Russia's northern Murmansk region, is the first governor to be detained for five years.
national.body:
The governor of Russia's northern Murmansk region has been arrested on corruption charges in the first detention of a regional leader for five years.

Andrei Chibis, 47, is suspected of embezzlement and misappropriation of more than a billion roubles ($12.2.m; £9.3m) set aside to build an Arctic highway, as well as a further 39m roubles from the Murmansk construction budget.

Chibis is reported to have been detained as he arrived on a visit to Moscow on Monday and was taken in for questioning.

He denies wrongdoing but has made no public comment. His wife Yevgenia Chibis said "anyone who knows our family understands how ridiculous this is".

In a post on social media, she said her husband sincerely believed in the Murmansk region and thanked people for their words of support: "We really need them right now."

Chibis worked for several years as deputy minister for construction and housing, before becoming governor of Murmansk in 2019.

Murmansk is a key military point for Russia in the Arctic and is home to the Russian navy's Northern fleet.

Chibis was re-elected two years ago after surviving a knife attack and is considered an active supporter of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Governors are seen as representing the Kremlin, and Vladimir Putin removed several in the months after the war began in February 2022.

national.summary: The explosion is the latest in a string of attacks on buildings housing the security forces and government offices.
national.body:
A car bomb has exploded in the central Colombian city of Villavicencio, injuring at least 23 people.

The explosive device was detonated in front of the offices of the regional government, in the city centre, damaging several buildings.

No group has so far admitted carrying out the attack - the latest in a series using explosives to target official buildings and security forces' headquarters.

Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella blamed "narcoterrorism", but gave no details. Armed criminal groups have recently stepped up attacks in what appears to be retaliation for an offensive ordered against them by De la Espriella.

Writing on social media, the president said that his government would "bluntly and forcefully" respond , external to "every drop of Colombian blood spilled".

Three weeks ago, three adults and a baby were killed in a car bomb attack near army barracks in Tolima province .

And earlier on Monday, drones dropped explosives on the police headquarters in the northern city of Cúcuta.

The car bomb in Villavicencio went off on Monday evening - the eve of the 10th anniversary of the signing of a peace deal between the government and left-wing rebels of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc), Colombia's largest guerrilla group.

MINA — Two people, found outside with with burns suffered from a house explosion on the French Creek-Mina Road near Findley Lake on Sunday, remain hospitalized at UPMC Pittsburgh.

Just after 6 p.m, firefighters responded to a call and found the house at 2170 French Creek-Mina Road fully engulfed in flames. Companies from Findley Lake, Sherman, Clymer, Panama, North Lake, Greenfield Township and Ripley responded and were on the scene until after midnight.

Stanley Hose Company Fire Chief Matt Oehleck was one of the first on the scene. “The house was fully involved when I got there and the roof had already collapsed,” he said. “There were two people in the front yard and they had severe burns.”

Findley Lake was the first to arrive with an engine, he added.

Findley Lake Fire Department Second Assistant Chief Jeff Park also noted two people with life-threatening injuries were found outside the house. They were taken to UPMC Hamot in Jamestown and then transported to Pittsburgh. Park said it is not known if the victims made it outside on their own or if they had been blown out by the explosion. “The debris field was hundreds of feet wide,” he said.

The explosion has been attributed to a propane leak, most likely in the basement of the house, Park said. It is not known how the leak occurred or how the propane built up sufficiently to cause such an explosion. “It’s possible the residents were away and had just come into the house,” he said. “All it would take is the flip of a light switch.”

Oehlbeck said Chautauqua County EMS and Findley Lake EMS were on the scene, as well as the Chautauqua County Fire Investigation Team and the Sheriff’s Office.

Both Oehlbeck and Park said the firefighters were on the scene until about 12:30 in the morning Monday. “It took more than four hours to put the fire out,” Oehlbeck said. “The house was a total loss.”

The latest withering letter to City Hall from Albany’s fiscal watchdogs concerns the 2027 budget proposed by Mayor Kate Wdowiasz and currently under review by the Common Council. “Based on the resu
local.body:
The Office of the State Comptroller has made yet another highly critical review of Dunkirk's finances.

The latest withering letter to City Hall from Albany's fiscal watchdogs concerns the 2027 budget proposed by Mayor Kate Wdowiasz and currently under review by the Common Council.

"Based on the results of our review, we determined that certain significant revenue and expenditure projections in the proposed budget were unreasonable," the letter states.

"In addition, we determined that of the 10 recommendations in our November 2025 budget review letter, the city fully implemented only three recommendations," OSC adds.

The items implemented were council review of certain appropriations identified in OSC's 2025 review; working to submit a report detailing the amount and cause of deficits; and close monitoring of revenues and expenditures, with timely and properly authorized budget adjustments as needed, throughout the year.

However, according to OSC, council did not make updating and correcting city accounting records a priority; did not properly establish a budget calendar; and did not ensure the 2026 budget was structurally balanced with realistic estimates before adopting it.

The letter repeatedly criticizes Dunkirk's finances on many levels. It notes, "Our (2027 budget) review was significantly limited by the city's incomplete, inaccurate and unreliable financial information, and by the responsiveness and willingness of certain council members and city officials to meet with our auditors. For example, we contacted all five council members, but only the councilman-at-large (Nick Weiser) and two other council members met with us."

OSC's letter continues, "Due to the poor financial information, we could not complete certain review procedures or adequately assess the reasonableness of significant 2026 revenue and expenditure projections and certain estimates in the proposed 2027 budget. In particular, we could not effectively analyze revenue and expenditure trends, and verify the assumptions supporting budget estimates, due to the city's unreliable accounting and financial information."

local.title: A local Mohawk woman connects with the land to preserve her indigenous roots
local.summary: For the month of November, WXXI is honoring the traditions and achievements of the Indigenous community for Native American Heritage Month.To commemorate the month, WXXI is sharing stories of local Indigenous people who are preserving their culture in their own way.
local.body:
This time of year, Jennie Brant spends most of her days in rubber boots prepping her farmland for the spring. During the colder months, the greenery fades, and the land becomes a barren sea of tan and beige.

"The last of the leaves fell this week," Brant said. "It's really a lot prettier before everything turns brown."

Enka:ri Farm , Brant admits, doesn’t look or operate like a typical farm. When she first purchased the farm nine years ago, Brant said it had been acres of corn and soy. Since then, she’s turned the farm into something a little more intrinsic.

She's designated a small number of acres to grow fruits and vegetables, but the rest of the land consists of overgrown wildflowers, native plants, and wildlife — all existing harmoniously.

"Part of the Native perspective would be our community is not just our human kin, but like all the beings," Brant said. "So preserving this space and creating this space has created this ecological system that's really beautiful and diverse."

Enka:ri means "it will ripen" in Mohawk. Brant said the name speaks to the faith and patience she uses to grow her produce, while highlighting her Indigenous roots and customs.

"We were all connected to the land at some point," Brant said. "It's about getting back there and doing the work to find your way back to it."

This summer, Brant helped launch Fresh Farmers Together — a grassroots nonprofit cooperative that helps farmers bring their produce and other products to the public market. Brant said costs have gone up so much, even something as simple as owning a table can be a barrier for some farmers.

Sara Jane Sion, 85, of Collins, NY passed away Sunday November 22, 2026 at her home.

She was born March 10, 1941 in North Collins, NY the daughter of the late Francis and Doris (Raecher) Winter.

On September 8, 1958 she married Daniel Sion who predeceased her on October 12, 2022.

She was a Beautician and hair stylist for many years.She was a member of St. Joseph's RC Church in Gowanda, NY, Altar and Rosary Society, member at Epiphany of Our Lord RC Church in Langford, NY and the Gowanda Moose.

Mrs. Sion was a Town of Collins Councilwoman and she also was an Election Inspector.

She is survived by three sons, Danny Sion of Collins, NY, Jeff (Mary) Sion of Lugoff, SC and Timothy (Sharon Urban) Sion of Hamburg, NY; and two daughters, Teresa (late Thomas) Powenski of Collins, NY and Tamara (Rodney) Utley of Perrysburg, NY; and 13 grandchildren, and 19 great grandchildren. Also surviving is a brother, Kenneth (Barb) Winter of Eden, NY; and a sister, Marcia (Raymond) Stromecki of Orchard Park, NY; and several nieces and nephews.

Besides her loving husband, she is predeceased by a son, Christopher Sion and a brother, Martin Winter.

Friends may call at the Mentley Funeral Home Inc. 105 East Main Street Gowanda, NY on Tuesday November 24, 2026 from 4pm – 6:30pm.

Thanksgiving is nearly upon us, when we will once again get to sharpen knives with our clueless relatives about national politics at the dinner table.

Hopefully, this year we may find some of our dear ones finally seeing the light, now that Donald Trump is a lame duck President, repudiated by Democrats and even members of his own party in the recent midterm elections.

"Why didn’t you hit me over the head with a frozen drumstick?"

Now, the final straw that many of them will be grasping is the notion that Donald Trump was sent to America by God, just as King Cyrus was sent to release the Jews from the Babylonian captivity in 538 BC.

Cyrus was a personal hero to many people, from Alexander the Great to David Ben-Gurion. Thomas Jefferson’s copy of "Cyropaedia," written about Cyrus’s career, shows substantial marginal markings that signify the degree of its influence on his drafting the Declaration of Independence.

Like Donald Trump, King Cyrus was a flawed man. At the age of 10, during a childhood game, he had the son of a nobleman beaten when he refused to obey his commands. Years later, after one of his horses drowned in the Gindarus River, a furious Cyrus set his army to spend the summer dividing the river into 360 channels.

According to the Greek historian Herodotus, Cyrus’s later years were marked by arrogance, which led to rash decisions. Did he by any chance impulsively deface the portraits of his predecessors in the palace gallery with crude, derogatory plaques? Trump did.

On the contrary, King Cyrus generally treated defeated rulers with remarkable clemency, often allowing local officials to retain power, in order to foster loyalty. But Donald Trump has fired hundreds of career government bureaucrats and replaced them with inexperienced loyalists - creating the first "deep state" in American history.

local.body:
WEBSTER -- Frewsburg/Falconer junior Anelia Pitts was seeded 21st in 1-meter diving heading into the New York State Public High School Athletic Association swimming and diving championships at Webster Aquatic Center this past weekend.

Pitts posted a score of 404.75 through her 11-dive program to place 18th overall, improving her seeding by three spots.

The winning score was turned in by Section V's June Piorkowski of Liverpool, who posted 481.60 points, just edging out Goshen's Kaylee Croughan with 475.85.

Section VI cracked the top 10 with Grand Island senior Kayla Rejewski at ninth with 431.70 points. Iroquois freshman Shea Jacobs earned 16th with a score of 408.90.

Southwestern/Jamestown senior Clarissa Hren was seeded 28th in the 200-yard individual medley and lived up to that with a time of 2:17.00 to earn 28th in the state. Ursuline junior Jane Chevalier posted the fastest time for the Federation title at 2:00.95, while Section VII's Long Beach junior Una Diaz won the state title with a time of 2:01.54.

The closest Section VI came to winning an event was Kenmore senior Amelia MacKinnon, who made the podium in both the 100-yard and 200-yard freestyles, taking fifth (52.06) and sixth (1:53.59), respectively.

local.body:
The Randolph girls soccer team once again dominated Chautauqua-Cattaraugus Athletic Association Division 2 with a perfect record, outscoring opponents 56-4 to win the league for a second year in a row.

The leader of that success in her first varsity season was eighth-grader Elsie Freeman, who paced the Cardinals offensively with 18 goals and nine assists from the midfield to earn the league's All-Conference Player of the Year honor.

Freeman was joined on the First Team by freshman forward Serena Smith, who scored 17 goals and eight assists, while senior defender Grace Arnold-Hill had a goal and two assists on First Team with the Cardinals keeping nine clean sheets. Senior Stella Smith was named the First-Team goalkeeper giving up only eight goals across all competitions for Randolph and making 71 saves on 79 shots faced with nine clean sheets.

Randolph earned Second-Team selections with junior defenders Kyler Patterson and Hannah Hill, while sophomore Ava Sears was picked as a midfielder. Sophomore defender Peyton Hale was Randolph's Individual Sportsmanship Award recipient.

Salamanca had a trio of sophomores named to the First Team with forward/midfielder Addison Earley pacing the squad with 19 goals and four assists, Ireland Fidurko adding six goals and 11 assists from the same position and Delaney Haley having a goal and two assists from defense with the Warriors keeping eight clean sheets and outscoring opponents 50-11 in league.

Salamanca added another three to the Second Team with senior midfielder Arleigh Chudy, sophomore defender Harper Ellis and sophomore midfielder Brielle Massagli. Senior defender Lily Vogle earned the Individual Sportsmanship Award for Salamanca.

Ellicottville also had three girls named to the First Team with senior defender Ava Fuller, who helped the Eagles outscore opponents 35-12 with eight clean sheets. Senior midfielder Eliza Murray scored 10 goals and two assists, and junior forward Juleana Lyon paced the squad with 11 goals and two assists.

Ellicottville added senior midfielders Ainsley Edwards and Juliana O'Connell to the Second Team along with sophomore defender Ella Weber. Sophomore forward Taylor Perks earned the Individual Sportsmanship Award for Ellicottville.

local.body:
With Thanksgiving only two days away, there is no question the north county region again came through to help neighbors for the holidays.

Within the last week, our newspaper has reported on donations collected by Brooks-TLC Hospital that will support FeedMore WNY partner organizations serving local communities in Chautauqua County. Those include the Boys and Girls Club of Northern Chautauqua County, Chautauqua County Rural Ministries Friendly Kitchen, Dunkirk City Schools 3 and 7, Dunkirk Conference Center, The Dunkirk Salvation Army, St. Elizabeth Ann Seton Food Closet and Dunkirk Middle and High School.

“We are proud to be part of Rock Out Hunger and grateful for the opportunity to give back to the communities we serve,” said Ken Morris, president of Brooks-TLC Hospital. “The generosity and enthusiasm demonstrated by our employees are proof of the commitment they have not only to providing exceptional care, but also to supporting our neighbors beyond the walls of our hospital. Every donation makes a difference and we are proud to see our team come together for such an important cause.”

In addition to Brooks-TLC, other community groups have donated to Chautauqua County Rural Ministry. Those include: Lakeshore Street Rod Association; the SUNY Fredonia boys' baseball team and community members from Pomfret and Fredonia during a weekend food drive.

“People in this county are very generous,” Street Rods President Dale Davis said.

local.summary: The city is currently without a contractor to dispose of the leaves residents collect, bag and set out on the curbside for crews to collect.
local.body: Buffalo does not have a way to dispose of leaves and the problem is piling up in a parking lot in North Buffalo. The city is currently without a contractor to dispose of the leaves residents collect, bag and set out on the curbside for crews to collect. Instead, the bags end up in a pile at the NFTA's LaSalle Station parking lot in North Buffalo. Buffalo's Deputy Mayor Benjamin Swanekamp tells me the pile is a holding station for the bags before being transported to a holding garage in South Buffalo. "Right now we have to either find a contractor willing to work with us, or as might be increasingly necessary, us to develop our own yard waste recycling program," Swanekamp said.The leaves were once dealt with by Geiter Done, a yard waste disposal company based in the Seneca Babcock neighborhood. But in 2024, the company was issued a notice of violation by the DEC after odor complaints. As a result, Swanekamp tells me the Buffalo Common Council did not approve a contract renewal with the company."When it came up for renewal, the Common Council rejected them two years in a row, so since then the city's been in the position of having to hold debris," Swanekamp said.So why doesn't the city just send all of this to a landfill? New York state regulations prohibit leaves and certain yard waste from being sent to landfills to prevent methane emissions. local.title: Holiday shopping rush brings increased concerns about package theft and scams
local.summary: Americans are expected to spend a record $275 billion shopping online this holiday season, creating plenty of opportunities for thieves and scammers.
local.body: With Black Friday just days away, the holiday shopping rush is about to kick into high gear. Americans are expected to spend a record $275 billion shopping online this holiday season, creating plenty of opportunities for thieves and scammers.A study by SafeWise estimates that more than 100 million packages were stolen nationwide in 2025. While that's down from the previous year, porch piracy remains a major concern.Meanwhile, the Federal Trade Commission says fake package delivery notifications are the most commonly reported type of text message scam.Amazon, the nation's largest online retailer, is preparing for the holiday rush by hiring more than 300,000 workers nationwide."This is our Super Bowl," Amazon spokesperson Owen Torres told 7 News.The company is offering advice to help customers protect their purchases.One recommendation is to take advantage of Amazon's package tracking tools, which allow customers to monitor deliveries and share tracking information with friends or family members who can retrieve packages if the customers aren't home.Customers can also provide specific delivery instructions, including asking drivers to leave packages in less visible locations."I kind of have the instructions to hide it behind one of my planters," Torres said. "It takes it away from street view and protects the packages out of sight."If a package is stolen, Amazon recommends reporting the theft to local police before contacting customer service through the Amazon app or website to explore possible remedies.Package theft isn't the only concern.Amazon says approximately 360,000 customers contact the company each year to ask whether an email, text message or phone call claiming to be from Amazon is legitimate.The company warns that scammers often create a sense of urgency, request personal information or demand payments through gift cards.Amazon recently introduced a new tool for its "Alexa for Shopping" AI assistant, which allows customers to ask whether a suspicious communication actually came from the company. Customers can access the feature through the Amazon app or Amazon.com.Amazon also recommends using its secure Locker delivery locations as an alternative to having packages left unattended on doorsteps.

local.body: Eight months after 30-year-old JohnLuc Jubert was killed in a crash on the Kensington Expressway, four people have been indicted on manslaughter charges. local.summary: As recent delays and a Delta outage rattle holiday plans, travelers at the Buffalo Niagara International Airport share their worries — but officials say operations are back to normal.
local.body: As recent delays and a Delta outage rattle holiday plans, travelers at the Buffalo Niagara International Airport share their worries — but officials say operations are back to normal.Recent flight delays have travelers heading home for Thanksgiving weekend worried about their journeys.I caught up with Emma Lipshultz as she arrived from Miami, flying alone for the first time with her 3-month-old daughter. She came to see her dad, who lives in Orchard Park. But with weeks of flight delays and Sunday's Delta outage, she was nervous about traveling for Thanksgiving."I definitely was nervous about that, but we were very happy that we made it," Lipshultz said.Her return trip is also on her mind."We're going back on Sunday, which is again a busy time to fly, so I'm a little bit nervous about that," Lipshultz said.Another traveler, headed home to Kansas City on a Delta flight after a conference in Canada, is also worrying about the recent flight disruptions."I heard horror stories about my colleagues and other friends who were traveling, and it's just pretty crazy when things like that happen," Dithi Banerjee said.Banerjee said the impact goes beyond passengers."It's not just the passengers. I feel for the airport employees. I feel for the airline employees, who really have to face the brunt of all of the anxiety and the disappointment," Banerjee said.NFTA spokesperson Kelly Khatib tells me operations at the Buffalo airport have been back to normal."Anytime that anyone's travel plans or wherever you're going is interrupted, it can be frustrating for people, but I think the biggest thing that people should remember is air travel is the safest way to go," Khatib stated. "You could be traveling out of the Buffalo airport, and everything is a-okay, but when you get to your second destination, if you have a stop in between, that might be different."The best advice if you're flying: download your airline's app and carry on your luggage if you can.
